name: Abdul Kahar Akond
role: Retired police officer and Pilkhana investigation officer
contribution: As a Criminal Investigation Department officer, Abdul Kahar Akond led the investigation into the 2009 Pilkhana mutiny and massacre and submitted a charge sheet against 824 accused in the murder case.
context: His work belongs to the post-incident prosecution and accountability process following the 25–26 February 2009 revolt at Bangladesh Rifles headquarters. Court records describe the evidence-gathering and witness-recording process, while rights reporting raised separate concerns about torture and the fairness of proceedings against some accused personnel.
impact: Akond's investigation became part of the evidentiary foundation for the Pilkhana trials and a continuing public debate about accountability. A 2013 trial-court judgment also ordered departmental action against him over allegations that his investigation had been biased in relation to one accused; those allegations should be distinguished from the court record of his investigative role.
highlight: CID investigation officer who led the 2009 Pilkhana case investigation and filed charges against 824 accused.
seoTitle: Abdul Kahar Akond: Pilkhana Investigation Officer
seoDescription: Learn about Abdul Kahar Akond's role as the Criminal Investigation Department officer who led the investigation into the 2009 Pilkhana mutiny case.
shortAnswer: Abdul Kahar Akond was the Criminal Investigation Department officer who led the investigation into the 2009 Pilkhana mutiny case and submitted charges against 824 accused.

faq.question: What was Abdul Kahar Akond's role in the Pilkhana case?
faq.answer: He served as the Criminal Investigation Department investigation officer and led the inquiry that resulted in a charge sheet against 824 accused in the murder case.

faq.question: Why is Abdul Kahar Akond's investigation debated?
faq.answer: The investigation was central to the prosecution, but a trial-court judgment ordered departmental action after finding his handling of one accused's case biased. Human rights reporting also documented broader concerns about torture and unfair trials; these concerns are not presented here as a complete finding about every part of his work.
